\[

\]

\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{-ix}}{x^2+a^2}\,dx=I
\]
by the substitution $x\mapsto -x$, since $x^2+a^2$ is even. Consequently,
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\cos x}{x^2+a^2}\,dx
=\frac12(I+I)=I=\frac{\pi e^{-a}}a.
\]
\end{proof}

\[

\]
For $R>a$, integrate $F$ over the positively oriented upper semicircle contour. The poles inside the contour are determined by $z^2+a^2=0$, namely $z=ia$ and $z=-ia$; only $ia$ lies in the upper half-plane. Since $F$ decays on the upper semicircle, its arc integral vanishes as $R\to\infty$. The residue theorem therefore yields
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{ix}}{x^2+a^2}\,dx
=2\pi i\operatorname{Res}_{z=ia}F(z).
\]
Because the pole is simple,
\[
\operatorname{Res}_{z=ia}F(z)
=\frac{e^{i(ia)}}{ia+ia}
=\frac{e^{-a}}{2ia},
\]
so
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{e^{ix}}{x^2+a^2}\,dx
=\frac{\pi e^{-a}}a.
\]
The imaginary part of this integral is zero because $\sin x/(x^2+a^2)$ is odd. Hence its real part equals the integral of the cosine term, and thus
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\cos x}{x^2+a^2}\,dx
=\frac{\pi e^{-a}}a.
\]
\end{proof}
